query: The Co-free FeNiCrMn system was selected to reduce cost while retaining the mechanical performance of equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi; prior work reported comparable or better mechanical properties after excluding Co. Research on FeNiCrMn has mainly addressed corrosion, while studies of related high- and medium-entropy alloys examined dynamic responses under tension or compression, different temperatures and strain rates, compositional changes, and the presence of cracks or voids. Those studies established that dynamic properties are sensitive to loading regime and material condition, but their different chemistries and defect states do not identify what governs FeNiCrMn. Under the constraints of retaining the Co-free composition and its strength–ductility balance, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis explains the dynamic behavior of solidified FeNiCrMn across temperature and strain-rate regimes? Define a controlled study capable of testing the hypothesis, its applicable boundaries, the prior findings that support it, and a result that would falsify it.

The sample began to yield, which means that dislocations started to occur and continued along the slip planes, generating double-layer HCP structures in the form of intrinsic stacking fault (ISF) (Figure 4 black arrows). Despite various experimental studies that have suggested that precipitation plays a significant role in yield strength and post-yield hardening, there still limited theoretical study has quantitively investigated the relationship. Therefore, a mesoscale model is urgently needed to elucidate the strengthening mechanisms of CoCrFeMnNi to improve its yield strength and post-yield behavior. Crystal plasticity finite element method (CPFEM) has been applied to study the plastic anisotropy and work hardening of aluminum alloys. CPEFM integrates the crystal plasticity theory with the finite element method and considers the interaction between the internal grains and the complex boundary conditions. This method enables the study of grain size effects and deformation behavior at complex stress fields and high strain rates. To further extend the ability of CPFEM to deal with precipitation, the hardening model used in this study utilized two dislocation densities: geometrically necessary dislocation density ρg and statistically stored dislocation density ρs.
